To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the lateralized auditory perception of spatially laterally placed sounds is not accompanied by the contralaterally biased processing in auditory cortex that is present for monaural sounds, and that the contralateral bias in the processing of monaural sounds decreases over time.

1) the degree of contrality of auditory cortex activity, as assessed by fMRI, was greater for monaural stimuli than for laterally perceived bimaural stimuli, and 2) the degree of auditory cortex contrality, as assessed by MEG, decreased across the poststimulus time course, going from the earliest M50 latency to the latest M200 latency.

lateralized auditory perception is not correlated with the contralaterally of processing in the auditory cortex, and that the contralateral auditory cortex is less active than the ipsilateral auditory cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of the perception of spatially localized sounds.
the neural mechanisms of spatial hearing and the neural basis of lateralized auditory perception.
the relationship between lateralized perception and the contralat-erality of processing in the auditory pathways, as revealed by fMRI and MEG.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a clear contralateral bias in the processing of monaural sounds and no contralaterally for the processing of binaural sounds with lateralized spatial perception.
the contralateral auditory system is the primary system for auditory perception and the ipsilateral auditory system is primarily a system for spatial processing.
the auditory pathways are contralateral in the sense that the contralateral auditory cortex is more strongly activated than the ipsilateral auditory cortex by monaurally presented sounds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the auditory system has a strong contralateral bias for monaural sounds and a much weaker bias for binaural sounds.
the auditory cortex is strongly contralateralized for monaural sounds, and this contralaterality decreases for laterally perceived bimodal sounds.
lateralized perception of binaural sounds does not involve contralateral auditory cortex, and that lateralized auditory cortex is involved in processing monaurally perceived sounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can measure lateralization in the human brain.
the auditory cortex is lateralized, with the left hemisphere dominant for processing of sounds from the right ear and vice versa for the right ear.
the brain’s ability to perceive a sound as being on one side or the other is not a direct reflection of the degree of processing that is occurring in the contralateral cortex.
